reel.title: Reports: new US tariffs on 16 economies | Leverage or cost?
reel.hook: REPORTS: NEW US TARIFFS ON [16 ECONOMIES]
reel.topic: New US Section 301 tariffs reported to be close for 16 economies, and what is and is not known. Reuters (three people with knowledge of the matter, speaking on Tuesday 24 Nov): the Trump administration is set to announce new tariffs on 16 trading partners after a probe into excess factory capacity; the announcement is 'expected imminently'; the duties would be 'specifically tailored to each country'; goods from Mexico and Norway are unlikely to see any immediate levies; ceilings agreed in trade deals would be honoured (15% for the EU, Japan and South Korea, 19% for Malaysia); China's 20% cap on second-term tariffs would be honoured 'as long as a trade truce with Beijing is extended', and if it expires the Chinese rate 'would rise to a higher level'; the truce 'runs until January 10'; the duties are 'meant to rebuild' the 'Liberation Day' tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February; the USTR and the White House did not respond to Reuters' queries. AP (two people familiar with the matter, 8:30 PM EST Tuesday): 'China, the European Union and 14 other economies'; rates 'not immediately clear'; on top of duties of 10% to 12.5% imposed in July on 60 trading partners over forced labour; the plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal; the USTR is expected to release the probe's results 'in the coming days'; the White House and USTR did not respond; 'Trump could veto any legislation' that overturns the tariffs. The 16, as the USTR listed them when it opened the investigations on 11 March 2026 under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act of 1974: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India (USTR release; KPMG; Reuters gives the same 16). Greer in the release: 'many U.S. trading partners are producing more goods than they can consume domestically'. Hearings began on 5 May (USTR; KPMG: 5 to 8 May). China's answer: foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Wednesday 25 Nov: 'The so-called overcapacity is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation'; Beijing 'stopped short of threatening retaliation' (Reuters). Politics: Democrats 'won majorities in both houses of Congress earlier this month'; ING: 'Without the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto', their ability to dismantle the tariffs 'will remain limited' (Reuters). Next: Trump and Xi 'are set to meet again at a G20 gathering in Miami' next month (Reuters; AP: the G20 in Doral, Florida). Markets on Wednesday morning: Reuters says global stocks were weighed on by the tariff prospect and by a tech-led rally running out of steam, 'with Nasdaq futures down over 2%'; CNBC at 4:45 AM ET via JBizNews: Nasdaq 100 futures -2.3%, S&P 500 futures -1.4%; Newsquawk at 05:25 EST: NQ -2.3%, ES -1.4%; TipRanks at 5:44 AM EST: -2.55% and -1.54%.
